## A parsimonious model of tax evasion through input overreporting {#sec-model}

Price-taking firms maximize expected after-tax profits. Firms choose their inputs $\{K_{it},L_{it},M_{it}\}$, capital, labor, and raw materials to produce output $Y_{it}$ given output and input prices $\{P_{t}, \rho_t, r_{it}, w_{it}\}$,  a common production function (@eq-prod-fn), and their productivity $\omega_{it}$. This is a characteristic of the production function literature, firms share a common technology, but differ in their productivity. 

$$
Y_{it}=K_{it}^{\alpha_k}L_{it}^{\alpha_L}M_{it}^{\beta}\exp(\omega_{it}+\varepsilon_{it})
$$ {#eq-prod-fn}

As standard in the literature, firms observe $\omega_{it}$ when they choose their inputs. This is the well-known endogeneity problem of simultaneity [@Griliches1995]. $\varepsilon_{it}$ is an error term. The error term is not part of the firms' information set.

In addition, firms can freely choose their materials in the current period, but capital and labor are either predetermined or dynamic. In practice what this means is that when it comes to choosing materials, firms face static optimization problem. 

The characteristic of the materials being flexible is what makes them more susceptible to be overreported. Capital can be audited more easily than materials. For example, the tax authority can verify the existence of capital goods in the firm's premises. In contrast, materials are consumed in the production process and are more difficult to verify.

Likewise, labor leaves a larger paper trail than materials because of payroll taxes and social security contributions. These additional taxes and contributions makes labor more costly to evade than materials. The incentive for firms is to underreport labor to evade payroll taxes and social security contributions, but this is not the focus of this paper.

In the model, firms can choose to overreport their inputs by an amount $e_{it}\equiv M^*-M\ge0$ to claim additional tax deductions and maximize expected after-tax profits. $M^*$ is the reported level of materials, while $M$ is the true level of materials.

Firms pay a tax rate $\tau$ on their revenues after deducting their materials costs. $\tau$ is, therefore, equivalent to a value-added tax (VAT) or corporate income tax (CIT), where firms can only claim deductions for their expenses on materials.

The tax authority audits firms at random and always detects misreporting if the firm engages in tax evasion and gets audited [@Allingham1972]. The probabiliy of detection is then, $q(e_{it},a)$; where $a$ represents the exogenous monitoring effort by the tax authority. The probability of detection is continuous and increasing in both of its arguments, $\frac{\partial q}{\partial e_{it}} > 0$ and $\frac{\partial q}{\partial a} > 0$. The more a firm overreports, the more likely it is to be detected. Likewise, the larger the efforts of the tax authority in monitoring suspicious behaviour of firms, the higher the probability of detection. Let's also assume that if the firm does not overreport, $e_{it}=0$, then it cannot be detected, $q(0,a)=0$.

The evasion cost $\kappa_i(e_{it})$ is increasing, $\kappa_i(e_{it})'>0$, and convex in the amount overreported, $\kappa''_i(e_{it})\ge0$. In addition, not overreporting is costless, $\kappa_i(0)=0$.  This cost represents the direct cost of overreporting such as acquiring fake invoices and resource cost of maintaining parallel accounting books to keep track of the true and reported costs. It might also represent indirect costs or losses of incurring in tax evasion. If the firms decides to evade, the evading cost is paid whether the firms is detected evading or not.

Finally, if tax evasion is detected, the tax authority imposes a penalty. Detected firms are fined with a rate of $\phi$ over the value of evaded taxes in addition to the true tax liability.

Firms, then, solve @eq-eva
$$
\begin{aligned}
  \max_{K_{it},L_{it},M_{it}, e_{it}} \big(1-q(e_{it},a)\big)&\bigg[P_t\mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon}[Y_{it}]-\rho_{t} M_{it}-r_tK_{it}-w_tL_{it}\\
  &-\tau\left(P_t\mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon}[Y_{it}]-\rho_{t} (M_{it}+e_{it})\right)-\kappa_i(e_{it})\bigg]\\
  +q(e_{it},a)&\bigg[(1-\tau)(P_t\mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon}[Y_{it}]-\rho_{t} M_{it})-r_tK_{it}-w_tL_{it}\\
  &-\kappa_i(e_{it})-\phi\rho_t\tau e_{it}\bigg] \\
  \text{s.t. }\; Y_{it}&=K_{it}^{\alpha_k}L_{it}^{\alpha_L}M_{it}^{\beta}\exp(\omega_{it}+\varepsilon_{it})
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-eva}



The firms' problem (@eq-eva) can be rewritten as follows,
$$
\begin{aligned}
  \max_{K_{it}, L_{it},M_{it},e_{it}} \mathbb{E}[\pi_{it}|\Gamma] = &(1-\tau)\left(P_t\mathbb{E}[Y_{it}]-\rho_{t} M_{it}\right)-r_tK_{it}-w_tL_{it}\\
  &+[1-q(e_{it}, a)]\left(\rho_{t}\tau e_{it}\right)
  -q(e_{it},a)\phi\rho_t\tau e_{it}-\kappa_i(e_{it}) \\
  \text{s.t. }\; Y_{it}&=K_{it}^{\alpha_k}L_{it}^{\alpha_L}M_{it}^{\beta}\exp(\omega_{it}+\varepsilon_{it})
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-eva-2}


An interior solution leads to following first-order conditions,

$$
\beta K_{it}^{\alpha_K}L_{it}^{\alpha_L}M_{it}^{\beta-1}\exp(\omega_{it})\mathcal{E}=\frac{\rho_{t}}{P_t}
$$ {#eq-foc-m}


$$
\tau\rho_t\left(1-(1+\phi)\left(q(e_{it}, a)+\frac{\partial q(e_{it}, a)}{\partial e_{it}} e_{it}\right)\right) =\kappa_i'(e_{it})
$$ {#eq-foc-e}

where $\mathcal{E}=\mathbb{E}[\exp(\varepsilon_{it})]$. 

Under random auditing, @eq-foc-m is the familiar optimality condition, where the left-hand side is the marginal product of materials and the right-hand side is the relative prices of materials.


To better understand the incentives to overreport inputs, we can rewrite @eq-foc-e in terms of the evasion elasticity of the probability of detection, $\xi_{q,e}=\frac{\partial q(e_{it}, a)}{\partial e_{it}}\frac{e_{it}}{q(e_{it}, a)}$, as follows,

$$
\tau\rho_t\bigg(1-(1+\phi)\left(1+\xi_{q,e}\right)q(e_{it}, a)\bigg) =\kappa_i'(e_{it})
$$ {#eq-foc-e-elas}

The left-hand side of @eq-foc-e-elas is the marginal benefit of tax evasion, while, the right-hand side is the marginal cost of evasion. The marginal benefit of evasion decreases with the evasion penalty $\phi$, the probability of detection $q(e_{it}, a)$, and the evasion elasticity of the probability of detection $\xi_{q,e}$. The marginal cost of evasion increases with the level of evasion because $\kappa'(e_{it})\ge0$.

Note that there could be firms that can optimally choose not to evade, $e_{it}=0$. Because no overreporting would be a corner solution, @eq-foc-e will not hold for these firms. For these firms, the marginal cost of tax evasion is greater than the marginal benefit for any non-zero level of tax evasion. This implies that for these firms, @eq-foc-e becomes,

$$
\tau\rho_t \le\kappa_i'(0)
$$ {#eq-foc-noeva}


### Parametrization and normalization

To calibrate the model, we need to parameterize the evasion cost function and the probability of detection function. Also, we would need to normalize some variables for which we do not have data.

To start, we can parametrize the probability of detection with an exponential cdf as follows,

$$
q(e_{it}, a)=1-\exp(-\lambda_0a e_{it})
$$ {#eq-prob-detect}

where $\lambda_0>0$ is a parameter that governs how quickly the probability of detection increases with the amount overreported and the monitoring effort of the tax authority.

Since we do not have data on the monitoring effort of the tax authority, we can normalize it to $a=1$. In addition, there was no penalty in Colombia for tax evasion during this period. If you were caught evading taxes, you only had to pay the evaded taxes. Thus, we can set $\phi=0$.

For the evasion cost function, we can use a linear function. We can allow for Corporations to have a greater marginal cost of evasion than the rest of the firms. Thus, we can write the evasion cost function as follows,

$$
\kappa_i(e_{it})=e_{it}(\gamma_0+\gamma_1 \mathbb{1}[i\in \text{Corp}])
$$ {#eq-eva-cost}

where $\gamma_0>0$ is the baseline marginal cost of evasion, and $\gamma_1\ge0$ is an additional marginal cost for Corporations. $\mathbb{1}[i\in \text{Corp}]$ is an indicator function that takes the value of 1 if firm $i$ is a Corporation and 0 otherwise.

### Estimating equations

For estimation purposes, we can simplify @eq-foc-m by multiplying by $M_{it}$ and dividing by $Y_{it}=K_{it}^{\alpha_k}L_{it}^{\alpha_L}M_{it}^{\beta}\exp(\omega_{it}+\varepsilon_{it})$. Then, by taking logs, this leads to the following expression,

$$
\ln\left(\frac{\rho_{t}M_{it}}{P_tY_{it}}\right) =\ln(\beta\mathcal{E})-\varepsilon_{it}
$$ {#eq-foc-m-simp} 

For the case of Colombia, what matters is the effective sales tax rate [see @sec-the-story]. The effective sales tax rate will vary by firm within an industry and over time depending on several firm characteristics such as size, juridical organization, share of exports and imports among others. Thus, we can use this rich variation and replace the statutory tax rate $\tau$ with the effective tax rate $\tau_{it}$.

Then, substituting the parametrizations of the probability of detection (@eq-prob-detect) and the evasion cost function (@eq-eva-cost) into @eq-foc-e leads to the following expression,

$$
\tau_{it}\rho_t\left(1-(1-\exp(-\lambda_0 e_{it})+\lambda_0 e_{it}\exp(-\lambda_0 e_{it}))\right) =\gamma_0
$$ 

Then, by simplifying and taking logs,

$$
\ln\left(\tau_{it}\rho_t\right) = \ln(\gamma_0) +\lambda_0 e_{it}-\ln(1-\lambda_0 e_{it})
$$ 

Moreover, we need to consider that what the econometrician observes is the reported intermediate inputs, $M^*_{it}=M_{it}+e_{it}$. However, because Corporations do not overreport, for them, $M^*_{it}=M_{it}$.

Thus, for Corporations, we have two equations,

$$
\ln\left(\frac{\rho_{t}M^*_{it}}{P_tY_{it}}\right) =\ln(\beta\mathcal{E})-\varepsilon_{it}
$$ {#eq-foc-m-corp}

$$
\tau_{it}\rho_t\le \gamma_0 + \gamma_1
$$ {#eq-foc-noeva-corp}

For the rest of the firms, we have,

$$
\ln\left(\frac{\rho_{t}(M^*_{it}-e_{it})}{P_tY_{it}}\right) =\ln(\beta\mathcal{E})-\varepsilon_{it}
$$ {#eq-foc-m-noncorp}

$$
\ln\left(\tau_{it}\rho_t\right) = \ln(\gamma_0) +\lambda_0 e_{it}-\ln(1-\lambda_0 e_{it})
$$ {#eq-foc-e-simp}


Alaternatively, following the measurement error literature, we can rewrite these equations in terms of the true inputs, with a centering condition.

The centering condition would be that the expected value of the tax evasion is zero for Corporations,

$$
\mathbb{E}[M^*_{it}-M_{it}|i\in \text{Corp}]=0
$$ {#eq-centering}

The other equations we can rewrite as,

$$
\mathbb{E}\left[\ln\left(\frac{\rho_{t}M_{it}}{P_tY_{it}}\right)\right] -\ln(\beta\mathcal{E})=0
$$ {#eq-foc-m-me}

$$
\mathbb{E}\left[\ln\left(\tau_{it}\rho_t\right) -\ln(\gamma_0) -\lambda_0 (M^*_{it}-M_{it})+\ln(1-\lambda_0 (M^*_{it}-M_{it}))|i\not\in \text{Corp}\right]=0
$$ {#eq-foc-e-noncorp-me}

$$
\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{1}[\ln(\tau_{it}\rho_t) -\ln(\gamma_0 + \gamma_1)\le0]-1|i\in \text{Corp}]=0
$$ {#eq-foc-e-corp-me}
